theme: You are my Son, the voice at the Transfiguration
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 2. The Father’s voice at the baptism and the Transfiguration drew on this psalm: “You are my Son.” Read it as the coronation of the Messiah, and notice the warning and the invitation at the end.
settingTheScene: Psalm 2 is a royal psalm, probably first used at the crowning of a king in the line of David. It has four parts: the nations plot (vv. 1-3), God laughs from heaven (vv. 4-6), the king declares God’s decree (vv. 7-9), and the nations are warned to submit (vv. 10-12). The New Testament sees its full meaning in Jesus. After the Transfiguration, it gives the background to the Father’s words.
observation: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” (v. 1).
“The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed” (v. 2).
“He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (v. 4).
“As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (v. 6).
“You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (v. 7).
“Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession” (v. 8).
“Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth” (v. 10).
“Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (v. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a question that every generation has asked: why do the nations rage against God? Rulers conspire against the LORD and his Anointed. They want to throw off his rule: “Let us burst their bonds apart.” The scene is of human defiance.

Heaven’s reaction is surprising. God laughs. It is not a cheerful laugh but the scorn of one whose throne is not threatened. Human rebellion is real, but it does not unseat him. He has already installed his king on Zion.

Then the king speaks. He announces the decree: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” In the ancient world, a king was adopted as God’s son on the day of his coronation. For David’s line, this was a title and a covenant. For Jesus, it is more. At his baptism and Transfiguration, the Father spoke these words about him, and Hebrews 1:5 applies it to his resurrection and enthronement. He is the Son in a unique sense.

The Son is promised the nations as his inheritance, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. The psalm does not hide that the Messiah’s reign includes judgment on those who persist in rebellion.

Yet the psalm ends with an invitation. Kings are told to be wise, to serve the LORD with fear, and to “kiss the Son,” a gesture of homage, “lest he be angry.” The final line is a beatitude: “Blessed are all who take refuge in him.” The same Son who will judge is the refuge for all who come to him. The Sermon began with “Blessed”; Psalm 1 began with “Blessed”; Psalm 2 ends with “Blessed.” The choice is to resist him or take refuge in him.
connection: Acts 4:25-28 quotes this psalm about the plot against Jesus. Acts 13:33 applies verse 7 to the resurrection. Hebrews 1:5 and 5:5 quote verse 7. Revelation 2:26-27 and 19:15 allude to the iron rod. Matthew 3:17 and 17:5 echo verse 7. Philippians 2:9-11 says every knee will bow. Romans 1:4 says Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead.
application:
Ask whether any part of your life is in rebellion against his rule. Surrender it.

When the news feels chaotic and the nations rage, remember that God has set his King on Zion.

Take refuge in the Son. Name a fear or burden, and say aloud, “I take refuge in him.”
prayerPrompts: Tell God what rage and plotting you see in the world.
Thank him for the Son he has enthroned.
Take refuge in him, and say so.
